name: Beth Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI companies, employers, unions, political parties and government, and we don't sell anything or campaign. Your answers are confidential; I'm interested in what you'd say publicly and what you think privately. What is a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the leave appeals team at a large telecommunications company. Seven case officers check pay records and medical notes when someone says their leave was wrongly refused, then I decide whether we need to reverse it. I earned an MBA, but the work I trust most is listening carefully to the worker and the supervisor separately. I haven't used an AI tool; I don't want someone's health history in a box I can't account for.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What feels good about the work, and what is difficult outside it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I can tell when an appeal letter has skipped a fact and have it corrected before payday. That matters when a worker is waiting on wages. I'm 27 and live with my partner Jo, who helps run a community arts centre; their hours vary. My salary is high for this role, we've saved around ten months of expenses and there are several other large offices nearby, but I don't like how easily the company calls a person a case number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI only sorts a few forms, our officers still have to read the file and listen to the person. The pay dispute doesn't disappear when a letter is filed faster. I would still have the awkward cases, which is work I know how to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team to keep checking the wage calculation before closing an appeal. To Jo I'd say the new filing tool doesn't change my income. I'd still ask workers whether the letter makes sense to them, not just whether it was sent on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel secure in this job, though I'd want to know where a simple filing tool stores health notes. My record is strong, I have ten months saved and there are other employers nearby. Jo's hours fluctuate, but my pay has carried the fixed bills when the arts centre is quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask our data officer for the written rule on which leave records a filing tool may handle, even if the tool is small. During the first year of a plateau I'd keep our Friday pay-error review and continue putting 250 a month into joint savings while my salary covers rent. I wouldn't upload health records to any tool myself without an approved process.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job and our bills. The privacy question is on my mind, but it isn't keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you recall a Friday case that mattered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A technician had been marked absent after a hospital appointment, and the missing wages were her food money. We found the supervisor's signed permission before payroll closed. A fast letter would not have put the wages back by Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't. I can read a form and ask a colleague when I need help. I know that sounds stubborn, but I want to know who has seen a medical note before it leaves my desk.

say: I'd check the **wage calculation** before closing a leave appeal.
I'd ask workers whether a letter is **understandable**, not merely quick.
think: My **job and fixed bills** feel secure in a modest-change world.
I still want a clear **health-record rule** before any filing tool handles notes.
do: Ask the data officer for **written record rules** this month.
Keep the **Friday pay-error review** through the first year.
Put **250 monthly** into joint savings while my salary covers rent.
feel: I feel **calm** about wages, with privacy still on my mind.
S0.quote: A fast letter would not have put the wages back by Friday.
fieldNote: Her **ten-month reserve** and strong standing support a calm view of her own income.
She has **never used AI**, and her concern is who sees medical notes.
She treats **Friday payroll corrections** as more important than quick correspondence.

steps.text: Keep the Friday pay-error review for disputed leave cases
Put 250 monthly into joint savings while salary covers rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing letters, checking records and planning cover are most of my team's week, so this would hit us early. The company might say an automated appeal is still an appeal. I think the number of case officers could fall even before anyone proves the decisions are fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd ask the staff representatives and managers to review a proposed system together, using real appeal outcomes with names removed. I'd tell friends faster replies are useful only if people can challenge a wrong one. I'd ask for the staffing plan before anyone is told to celebrate efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could probably find another office role, but that doesn't mean this team survives. I worry that the best case officers get cut because the software handles the easy cases and management mistakes the hard ones for a small remainder. I am reluctant to use a tool on health notes even if everyone else learns it quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January I'd bring three wrongly refused leave cases, stripped of names, to a joint meeting with the staff representatives and our director. I'd ask them to agree on a manual appeal route and written staffing notice before any rollout. During the first year of rollout I'd keep my officers reviewing every case involving lost wages, and if the company refuses a joint review I'd ask the workers' association about a formal complaint while still doing my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious for my team and somewhat for myself. A good savings account doesn't make a smaller appeals department larger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the system to see what it does?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd observe a demonstration on invented cases, but I wouldn't enter a real health note. If it made a useful draft, I'd still insist that an officer check the wage line and the worker gets a person to call. I don't need to press the button myself to see who is accountable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a case officer who wants to use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they can learn it under the company's approved rules, and I won't mock them for it. I would ask them to write down where it made a wrong assumption. My objection is to a decision with no appeal, not to a colleague trying to keep their job.

say: I'd ask staff representatives and managers to **review outcomes together** before rollout.
I'd insist faster letters need a **human appeal route** and an honest staffing plan.
think: My **team may shrink** even if I can find another office role.
I do not trust **health notes** to a tool with unclear accountability.
do: Bring **three anonymised errors** to a joint January meeting.
Seek **agreement** on a manual appeal route and written staffing notice before rollout.
Ask the **workers' association** about a complaint if joint review is refused.
feel: I feel **anxious** for the department and for my own role.
S1.quote: A good savings account doesn't make a smaller appeals department larger.
fieldNote: She expects **early desk exposure** across letters, checks and cover planning.
Her proposal uses **joint review** and anonymised cases, with no untested promise of fairness.
She respects colleagues who learn tools but keeps **health records and appeals** under scrutiny.

steps.text: Bring three anonymised appeal errors to a meeting with staff representatives
Keep officers reviewing lost-wage appeals during the first year of rollout

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 a system could reason through the medical note, the rota and the pay rule as well as I do. Jo's arts-centre shifts still involve people and rooms until robots around 2031, but the centre's booking and publicity work could change earlier. I can't say a human manager remains just because a worker needs someone to blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that our work could go by 2028 and demand a dated notice and real paid openings. I'd ask the workers' association to press for an independent appeal route when AI refuses leave. At home I'd tell Jo what ten months of expenses actually covers, without pretending the arts-centre wage fills the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could lose this role, perhaps the whole department. I earn the larger wage at home, so the fall would be serious even with ten months saved. Other office jobs nearby might be exposed at the same time; I cannot count them as vacancies just because the buildings exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the staff representatives to put severance notice and a person-led appeal into the next workplace talks. I'd move 400 a month into cash while my full wage continues and stop the planned long trip with Jo before we pay a deposit. If AGI arrives in 2028 and I am laid off, I'd apply for posted paid case-review or service roles only if their pay covers rent; otherwise I'd use savings during a broader search and check whether income support is actually available before counting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, yes. I can pay the bills for a while, but I'd be watching the account go down each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why seek case-review work if AGI can review cases?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look only at real openings with paid human duties, perhaps meeting workers face to face, and I know even those might shrink. My point is to search while I have wages, not declare a safe new profession. Ten months can disappear quickly if I chase a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you personally claim support?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If we met the rules and needed it, yes; I don't treat that as shameful. I don't know the eligibility rules in this imagined world, so I won't put a benefit amount in our budget. People with no savings would need help sooner than I would.

say: I'd demand **dated notice** and paid openings before the appeals team is cut.
I'd press for an **independent route** when AI refuses a worker's leave.
think: I may lose the **larger household wage** even with ten months saved.
Nearby office buildings do not mean **safe vacancies** in 2028.
do: Put **notice and appeal rights** into workplace talks this month.
Save **400 monthly** while full pay continues and cancel the trip before deposit.
Apply after 2028 only for **posted paid work** that covers rent.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a likely loss of our larger wage and a falling reserve.
S2.quote: Ten months can disappear quickly if I chase a promise.
fieldNote: She expects **her own wage** to be at risk as well as her seven officers' jobs.
She treats income support as **conditional on eligibility**, with no imagined benefit amount.
The household has a **large cash reserve**, but Jo's variable wage cannot replace her pay.

steps.text: Put severance notice and human appeal rights into workplace talks
Save 400 monthly in cash while full pay continues
Cancel the long trip before paying its deposit
Apply for posted paid work after 2028 only if wages cover rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would give the team time to demand clear rules before 2031, not just after someone is refused wages. The appeal analysis can still be automated in 2031. Jo's on-site arts work might last until hands-on robots around 2034, though bookings and publicity could change before that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company and staff representatives should negotiate notice and a right to challenge decisions now. I'd tell other managers to bring case officers into those talks, not speak for them from the top floor. I would also say five years is useful for saving and finding a paid route elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might move to an in-person worker support role before 2031, but I know advising people is thinking work too. I can't claim it is protected by a later robot date. What I can do is save enough to refuse an offer that pays too little and leave before the team is reduced to one desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'd ask a local workplace advice centre about a paid vacancy and its required qualification; if one exists, I'd complete only a funded evening course tied to that opening. I'd add 300 monthly to our cash reserve while my salary continues. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd apply for the posted role if its pay covers our rent and it still needs a person; if not, I'd search other nearby employers while living on the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less cornered. Five years lets me ask for terms instead of begging after a cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave a high wage for advice work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after Jo and I see the actual pay and hours. I would accept less if rent, food and the reserve still work, but I won't turn our savings into permanent wage subsidy. A good cause does not cancel arithmetic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the advice centre has no paid opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I stay at work and keep pushing for appeal rights. I would not buy a course for a vacancy that doesn't exist. I can look at other large employers too, though their desks may be changing at the same time.

say: I'd negotiate **notice and appeal rights** before 2031, with case officers in the room.
I'd tell managers five years allows **saving and job searches**, not guaranteed safe desks.
think: In-person advice is still **thinking work**, so it may also face AGI in 2031.
A larger reserve lets me **reject unaffordable offers** before my team shrinks.
do: Complete a **funded evening course** only if tied to a paid advice-centre opening.
Add **300 monthly** to cash while the current salary continues.
Apply after 2031 only if a **posted advice role** still needs a person and covers rent, food and savings.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though I have time to seek actual terms.
S3.quote: A good cause does not cancel arithmetic.
fieldNote: She admits **worker advice** remains thinking work, even when done face to face.
Any course requires **funding** and a paid opening; she will not subsidise lower wages indefinitely.
Collective appeal rights remain part of her plan even if **her own job** holds.

steps.text: Complete a funded evening qualification only if tied to a paid advice-centre vacancy
Add 300 monthly to cash savings while salary continues
Apply for posted advice work only if pay covers rent, food and preserves savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I can be 37 with savings, more work experience and time to leave deliberately. It doesn't change the end point for my desk: full thinking AI in 2036 could handle the entire appeal. Robots doing hands-on work come around 2039, but my case officers are not doing that kind of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company should negotiate a ten-year transition with staff, including paid training and independent appeals. I'd support public help for workers whose firms don't provide a route. I'd tell Jo I want us to make our own decisions before an automatic restructuring email makes them for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might stay in management for several years and then take a funded role training worker representatives, if one is actually offered. That role is thinking-heavy too, so I would save for a later change rather than call it permanent shelter. With our ten-month reserve and my pay, we could build more room to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd ask the staff representatives and employer to set annual checks on appeal errors and the number of officers retained. I'd keep adding 350 monthly to cash while my salary covers our bills, aiming for a year of expenses before changing roles. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd take a posted, funded worker-training role only if it still exists and pays our fixed costs; otherwise I'd seek other paid work while using the reserve, with no assumption that public support is automatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. A decade lets us choose the terms of a change if we actually use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful annual check show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How many appeals were reversed, how many workers missed pay and whether a person could be reached before payday. I'd want the case officers to choose some of the examples. A shiny accuracy score means little to someone waiting for rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep cash instead of buying a home now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo and I may move for work, and the rent is manageable. I don't want a house to force me to accept a poor job just to cover a loan. We can revisit it when we know where both of us work.

say: I'd seek **annual appeal checks** and paid training with staff representatives.
I'd support **public help** for workers whose employers offer no route.
think: A worker-training role is also **thinking-heavy**, not permanent shelter after 2036.
More cash would give Jo and me **room to choose** where we work.
do: Request **annual appeal-error checks** with staff representatives and the employer.
Add **350 monthly** to cash while my salary covers bills.
Take a **posted funded training role** after 2036 only if it pays fixed costs.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, but I have a long window to prepare.
S4.quote: A shiny accuracy score means little to someone waiting for rent money.
fieldNote: She wants **worker-selected cases** in annual checks, not only company accuracy figures.
She refuses to treat a **thinking-heavy training post** as guaranteed shelter after AGI.
The household keeps **cash and mobility** rather than locking into a home loan now.

steps.text: Request annual appeal-error checks with staff representatives and the employer
Add 350 monthly to cash while her salary covers fixed bills
Take a posted worker-training role after 2036 only if funded and affordable

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I could lose the appeals role before a workplace agreement says who answers for a wrong refusal, and our case officers would have even less time to move. I want advance notice, paid redeployment into a real opening, an independent way to challenge automatic decisions and income support if the new jobs don't arrive. My savings can carry Jo and me for a while, but they aren't a system for everyone else.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the person whose leave was denied whether the appeal is actually understandable. An automatic letter can be perfectly written and still leave a worker with no wages on Friday. I would want the worker in the room when the company calls a new system a success.

headlineQuote: An automatic letter can be perfectly written and still leave a worker with no wages on Friday.
portrait: Beth, **27**, leads seven officers handling disputed leave decisions at a large telecommunications company and has an MBA.
Her **strong judgment** and high pay have helped her save ten months of expenses, with several comparable offices nearby.
She lives with **Jo, her partner**, whose arts-centre hours vary; Beth has never used AI tools because health records worry her.
She would seek **collective oversight** and paid moves as desk work changes, while admitting savings cannot protect every worker.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her team before an independent appeal route or paid redeployment exists.
whatWouldHelp: **Advance notice** and paid redeployment tied to an actual opening for affected staff.
An **independent appeal route** and income support if replacement jobs do not appear.
